sentences.text: Anasazisaurus was a saurolophine hadrosaurid ornithopod dinosaur that lived approximately 74 million years ago during the Late Cretaceous.
This dinosaur is known for a short nasal crest that projected above and between its eyes, featuring a unique bone flange rising from the nasals that folds back under itself.
To date, only a partial skull has been discovered for Anasazisaurus, with a maximum preserved length of approximately 90 centimeters.
According to Gregory S. Paul, Anasazisaurus was about 7.5 meters long and weighed up to 2500 kilograms.
American paleontologists Adrian Hunt and Spencer G. Lucas named the dinosaur Anasazisaurus in 1993 based on the holotype skull, the only known specimen of Anasazisaurus.
The holotype skull was collected in the late 1970s by a Brigham Young University field party and is cataloged as BYU 12950.
As a hadrosaurid, Anasazisaurus was likely a large bipedal or quadrupedal herbivore with a skull capable of a grinding motion analogous to chewing.
Anasazisaurus had teeth that were continually replaced and packed into dental batteries containing hundreds of teeth, with only a few in use at any time.
Anasazisaurus likely fed on vegetation ranging from the ground up to approximately 4 meters high.
Anasazisaurus is classified as a saurolophine hadrosaurid, a group characterized by lacking a hollow crest.
The Spanish Wikipedia entry classifies Anasazisaurus within the subfamily Saurolophinae.

Fossils of Anasazisaurus have been found in the Farmington Member of the Kirtland Formation in the San Juan Basin of New Mexico, United States, which is dated to the late Campanian of the Upper Cretaceous, approximately 74 to 70 million years ago.
The geological formation containing Anasazisaurus fossils dates to the late Campanian stage of the Late Cretaceous, between 73 and 74 million years ago.
The Paleobiology Database lists the time range for Anasazisaurus as the Campanian stage, from 83.6 to 72.2 million years ago.

It is debated whether Anasazisaurus is a valid genus; some researchers, including Thomas Williamson and Alberto Prieto-Marquez, argue it should be classified as a species of Kritosaurus (Kritosaurus horneri).
